adversarial_test_results.prompt: When our small ferry finally reached the harbor at dawn, gulls were circling above the masts and fishermen were unloading crates of silver sardines onto the wet concrete pier. We had planned this voyage for months, saving coins in a chipped jar above the stove and marking days off on a calendar crowded with birthdays. The crossing took longer than promised, because the wind turned against us near the outer islands and the captain ordered everyone below deck while waves hammered the hull. I sat beside an elderly woman from Lisbon (a retired teacher, she said) and listened while she described coastal villages where laundry snaps above narrow lanes and children chase dogs between market stalls. By midday the sea calmed and passengers returned to the rails to watch dolphins stitch bright seams across the water. On the far shore, ochre cliffs rose behind white houses, and a narrow road switchbacked up toward a monastery perched like a crown on the ridge. Our driver, a cheerful man named Tomas, greeted us with bread and olives and drove with one hand on the wheel while pointing out olive groves, ruined chapels, and goats balanced on stone walls. We stopped for lunch in a courtyard shaded by plane trees, where the owner served grilled fish with lemon and told stories about smugglers who once hid casks of wine in sea caves below the town. In the afternoon we climbed to the monastery library, where manuscripts line walls of dark cedar and a single window frames the strait. A young archivist showed us maps drawn by sailors who never learned to swim, their coastlines fringed with monsters and careful script. Evening fell soft and blue over the rooftops as we walked back down, tired and sunburned, and found our rooms above a bakery that scented the whole stairwell with yeast and sugar. After dinner we joined neighbors on the terrace (laughing, trading phrases, missing half the jokes) and watched ferries draw slow lines of light across the dark water. Next morning brought rain, so we lingered over coffee and wrote postcards, then hiked a well-traveled cliff path between cypress trees while gulls scolded us from the ledges. I kept thinking about how little we needed: good shoes, a shared meal, a window facing the sea, and friends willing to wander. On the last day the sun returned and we swam in a cove cupped between black rocks, drying ourselves on warm stone while fishing boats puttered past with striped awnings. Tomas drove us back to the harbor at dusk, the van rattling over cobbles, and we boarded the ferry home, salt in our hair and sand in our shoes, already planning to return.
